title: Electrodeposited Cu2O Films on Gas Diffusion Layers for Selective CO2 Electroreduction to Ethylene in an Alkaline Flow Electrolyzer
abstract: Novel electrodes for the electroreduction of CO2 were prepared by the electrodeposition of copper (I) oxide (Cu2O) catalytic films on a gas diffusion layer. Different electrodes were prepared by varying the deposition time, corresponding to catalyst loadings of 0.37, 0.74, 2.22, 3.70 mgcm 2 and a total charge density of 0.5, 1, 3, and 5 Ccm , respectively. The electrodes were characterized with SEM, XRD, and UPD. The effect of catalyst loading on the selectivity towards ethylene was investigated in an alkaline flow electrolyzer under ambient conditions. The electrodes were found to be highly selective (> 60%) towards ethylene. The 1 Ccm 2 electrode reached Faradaic efficiency values as high as 67% at industrially relevant current densities of 183 mAcm , 0.8 V cathode overpotential and 36% cell energy efficiency. This performance was attributed to the interplaying role of applied potential, local pH, availability of active sites, and reduced CO2 mass transport limitations.

Novel electrodes for the electroreduction of CO2 were prepared by the electrodeposition of copper (I) oxide (Cu2O) catalytic films on a gas diffusion layer. Different electrodes were prepared by varying the deposition time, corresponding to catalyst loadings of 0.37, 0.74, 2.22, 3.70 mgcm 2 and a total charge density of 0.5, 1, 3, and 5 Ccm 2, respectively. The electrodes were characterized with SEM, XRD, and UPD. The effect of catalyst loading on the selectivity towards ethylene was investigated in an alkaline flow electrolyzer under ambient conditions. The electrodes were found to be highly selective (> 60%) towards ethylene. The 1 Ccm 2 electrode reached Faradaic efficiency values as high as 67% at industrially relevant current densities of 183 mAcm 2, 0.8 V cathode overpotential and 36% cell energy efficiency. This performance was attributed to the interplaying role of applied potential, local pH, availability of active sites, and reduced CO2 mass transport limitations.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electroreduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to fuels and chemicals has been attracting increased interest as the process can potentially provide a storage solution for intermittent renewable electricity while mitigating CO2 emissions. CO2 can be electrochemically reduced to a wide variety of molecules, including carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), ethanol (C2H5OH) and formic acid (HCOOH). [1]
In previous studies, a wide variety of metal catalysts have been tested for their selectivity and activity towards CO2 electroreduction products. Transition metals like gold, silver, and zinc were found to be selective towards CO, whereas lead and tin were selective towards HCOOH. Copper catalysts were found to be uniquely capable of producing C2 products (C2H4, C2H5OH) through the electroreduction of CO2. [1a,2]
The focus of this study is the electroreduction of CO2 to C2H4, which is a product of great industrial interest due to the high value and large demand in the current chemicals’ infrastructure. Previous literature studies have shown the selectivity of CO2 electroreduction towards C2H4 to be dependent on the electrolyte (anion and cation type, concentration, pH), catalyst (morphology, surface structure, and presence of other metals), operating voltage, and pressure.[3] Along these lines, a wide variety of Cu-based catalysts have been tested and examined
for their performance and selectivity, including copper oxide fibres, films, nanoparticles, and alloys.[2a,4]
Note that most academic catalyst testing is performed in a half-reaction electrochemical cell by bubbling CO2 and saturating the electrolyte. This results in low current densities due to the relatively low concentration of CO2 that can be dissolved in the electrolyte (~35 mM under ambient conditions and neutral pH).[1a,3c,d,5] Recently, researchers have reported moderate to high current densities (200–600 mAcm 2) using gas diffusion layers (GDL’s) as a substrate for the catalyst,[6] allowing CO2 to be supplied to the catalyst in the gas phase.[3a,b,e,6] Catalyst coated GDLs (also known as gas diffusion electrodes – GDE’s) incorporated within flow electrolyzers under alkaline conditions have shown improved performance in terms of selectivity and current densities. C2H4 selectivity up to 70% has been reported by Dinh et al. at 100 mAcm 2 but at a high pH of 10 M KOH.[3a]
Ma et al. reported a selectivity as high as 45% at about 150 mAcm 2,[3e] and 60% at 300 mAcm 2 was reported by Hoang et al. but with a bimetallic catalyst of Cu Ag rather than plain Cu.[3b] A higher selectivity of about 80% towards C2H4 has also been reported but at a relatively low current density (~ 54 mAcm 2).[7]
In this work, we report the selective and active electroreduction of CO2, affording up to 67% C2H4 at current densities about 183 mAcm 2, on copper (I) oxide (Cu2O) derived catalyst electrodeposited on GDLs. Further, the effect of copper catalyst loading in terms of selectivity and activity towards C2H4 in an alkaline flow electrolyzer is reported.

The deposition was performed at a fixed current density of 0.8 mAcm 2 at pH 12 and a controlled temperature of 60 °C. X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed the deposition of a Cu2O layer with a selective (111) orientation, consistent with previous electrodeposition studies performed at pH 12 (Figure S3, a).[3c,8a,9] Electrodes with four different loadings were prepared by varying the deposition time until a total charge of 0.5 Ccm 2, 1 Ccm 2, 3 Ccm 2, or 5 Ccm
2 was applied, corresponding to a theoretical catalyst loading ranging from 0.37 to 3.7 mgcm 2 (Table 1).
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis, performed exsitu after the electrodeposition, showed that the 0.5 Ccm 2
applied charge was not enough to cover the whole surface of the GDL and produce a uniform catalyst layer on top of the substrate (Figure 1a). For an applied charge of 1 Ccm 2 the GDL area was found to be mostly covered with catalyst particles, however, as is apparent from Figure 1b, relatively small areas of the support still seem to be exposed. For an applied charge of 3 and 5 Ccm 2, the GDL area was visually fully covered, Figure 1c and 1d, respectively. SEM images also show increased crystal sizes when increasing the catalyst layer loading.
The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was measured using the underpotential deposition of lead (PbUPD), a method described in the experimental section.[10] The ECSA depends on the surface coverage and on the size of the crystals, such that it increases when a higher percentage of GDL surface is covered and decreases when bigger crystals are deposited. These dependences explain the highest ECSA of the sample prepared with 3 Ccm 2 (Table 1). The ECSA corresponding to the sample prepared with 0.5 Ccm 2 could not be attained due to a flat CV response of the sample, even after repetitive experiments (Figure S4).
The electroreduction of CO2 was performed in a flow electrolyzer set up, reported by Kenis et al.[11] (Figure S1), in a potentiostatic mode (constant cell voltages) with 1 M KOH as the electrolyte. The cathode outlet gas was analyzed with online gas chromatography (GC). Off-line GC and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis were performed to detect the liquid products. At the start of the experiments a cell voltage of 2.2 V was applied, leading to reduction of the catalyst to Cu0, as confirmed by XRD (Figure S3, b). Performance measurements were taken after stabilizing the current for at least 300 seconds. All potentials reported in this work are the actual measured values without any iR correction unless stated otherwise.
Figure 2 reports the current density for C2H4, CO, hydrogen (H2), and other products detected as a function of the cell
voltage for each catalyst loading tested. Other products mainly refer to HCOOH (1–2%), C2H5OH (1–10%), CH4 (1–4%), propylene (1–2%) and traces of 1-propanol, oxalic acid, acetic acid, ethane and allyl alcohol (see Table S3).
Faradaic efficiencies towards C2H4 up to 60% were obtained for all samples (Figure 3). The reported values are an average of 3 measurements, with narrow standard deviation indicating a high level of repeatability (Figure S8). The 0.5 Ccm 2 sample reached up to 65% FE to C2H4 at a cathode overpotential of 0.7 V but at a relatively low current density (72 mAcm 2). At

The HER takes place at the exposed carbon subsurface since the surface of the electrode is not completely covered with a uniform layer of Cu2O (Figure 1a). The 0.5 Ccm
2 sample doesn’t have enough active sites to sustain the CO coverages required for C2H4 production. Figure S6 also shows that the partial current density of H2 goes up dramatically at high cathode potentials. For the 1 Ccm 2 electrode, the Faradaic efficiency reaches values of 65% and stays constant for cathode overpotentials more negative than 0.7 V, resulting in the highest C2H4 production rate reported in this study (Table S2), corresponding to a partial current density above 120 mAcm 2 (Figure S6). Under these conditions, cell energy efficiency is 35% and energy efficiency for C2H4 is 24% (see supplementary information for calculation method).
Similarly, for the 3 Ccm 2 electrode the Faradaic efficiency is as high as 63% at 0.75 V cathode overpotential, corresponding to a partial current density for ethylene production of 99 mAcm 2, cell energy efficiency of 40%, and energy efficiency for C2H4 equal to 26%. Up to 2.8 V cell voltage, the 3 Ccm 2 electrode gives the highest current density presumably because of the highest active surface area, as measured by PbUPD (Table 1). Looking at Figure 3b the Faradaic efficiency for C2H4 for cathode potential up to 0.6 V vs. RHE are similar for both 0.5 and 1 Ccm 2 indicating a kinetically limited system that can be related to either CO production or C C coupling.
The highest Faradaic efficiency to C2H4 reached by the 5 Ccm 2 sample was 54% at 0.75 V cathode overpotential, resulting in a partial current density to C2H4 of 83 mAcm
2, cell energy efficiency of 40% and energy efficiency for C2H4 equal to 22%. The lower Faradaic efficiency compared to the 1 C and 3 Ccm 2 sample can be explained by the combination of lower ECSA and thicker catalyst layer that increases the CO2 mass transport limitations.
Previous reports from Dinh et al. show that thinner electrodes should have a higher CO2 to H2O ratio promoting the CO2RR over the HER but at the same time higher ECSA is needed in order to support high current densities.[3a] Looking at Figure 2 and at cell voltages from 2.2 V to 2.8 V, the partial current density for C2H4 production shows a similar trend to the
measured ECSA (Table 1); an increasing value from the 0.5 to 3 Ccm 2 sample and a decrease for the 5 Ccm 2 sample. At cell voltages more negative than 2.8 V, flooding (electrolyte crossover to the gas phase) caused the interruption of the experiment for the 3 and 5 Ccm 2 samples.
As already mentioned, the XRD patterns obtained for all samples after the CO2 electroreduction reaction show a preferential Cu (111) orientation (Figure S3b). This is in accordance with the findings of Schouten et al.[5a] that showed C2H4 formation on Cu (111) surfaces to proceed via the hydrogeneration of CO, at cathode potentials of 0.4 V vs. RHE and pH 13, suggesting a potential driven activation of the Cu (111) surface. This pathway is believed to be the one that produces C2H4 at higher (more negative) than 10 mAcm 2 current densities, occurring at both the Cu (111) and Cu (100) facets.[12]
The C2H4 increase at higher current densities is accompanied by a constant decrease of the CO selectivity at all the catalyst loadings tested (Figure S8), suggesting CO to be a key intermediate for this reaction, in accordance to many mechanistic studies proposed so far.[3d,g,5a,12–13]
No systematic durability studies were conducted in this work, but a decrease of the performance (Faradaic efficiency and product distribution, with increased HER) was observed after 1-hour operation at constant current (Figure S10). This might be due to catalyst deactivation, insoluble carbonate/ bicarbonate salts precipitations in the GDL preventing CO2 from reaching the catalyst surface, increased hydrophilicity of the GDL causing flooding of the electrode, or mechanical failure of the electrodes. SEM images after CO2 electrochemical reduction show the appearance of cracks on the electrode surface, exposing significantly the GDL (Figure S2b and S2c). Exposed carbon might explain an increased selectivity towards HER.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text:
Concluding, in this study, the highest selectivity to C2H4 of 67% under industrial relevant current densities, up to 183 mAcm 2, is reported at 0.8 V cathode overpotential. Selectivity was shown to be dependent on the applied potential, the current density, availability of Cu active sites (GDL coverage) and CO2 availability at the catalyst surface (mass transfer). The C2H4 selectivity was highest at intermediate catalyst loadings, with H2 selectivity increasing at higher loadings. The highest selectivity to C2H4 was obtained with a catalyst prepared with 1 Ccm 2 Cu2O electrodeposited on the GDL, reflecting effective CO2 mass transport through the electrode and the availability of active surface sites. The results presented in this work thus provide an improved understanding of CO2 electroreduction and the factors affecting selectivity towards C2H4, in particular the effect of catalyst loading on industrially relevant performance.

sections.heading: Cathode Preparation
sections.text:
The electrodes used as cathodes were synthesized with the method of electrodeposition using a GDL substrate. The desired GDEs were prepared by applying a fixed current in a 0.5 M CuSO4 solution (VWR chemicals) containing 3.0 M lactic acid (VWR Chemicals) and NaOH (pellets, Merck).[3c,8b] Cu2O films were electrodeposited via the reduction of the copper (II) lactate (Cu(CH3CHOHCOO)2) complex in an alkaline solution of pH 12. The lactic acid was added in the solution to form Cu(CH3CHOHCOO)2 preventing precipitation of Cu (OH)2 in the basic electrolyte solution. By complexing with the lactate ion, copper was stabilized, and the pH was raised to alkaline values by adding NaOH, at a controlled temperature of 60 °C. The formed complex was reduced to CuOH, which was further transformed to Cu2O upon dehydration.

The electrodes used in the setup were a Pt mesh (99.9%, Alfa Aesar) counter electrode, Ag/AgCl (Metrohm, stored in 3 M KCl) reference electrode, and a 5 cm2 gas diffusion layer (Sigracet 29BC, FuelCellStore) working electrode. The deposition was performed at a fixed current of 0.8 mA until a total charge of 0.5 Ccm 2, 1 Ccm 2, 3 Ccm 2, or 5 Ccm 2 was passed. The catalyst loading obtained in this preparation carried out in a galvanostatic mode, was determined by the duration of the experiment, hence the total charge passed through the electrode.[3g] After the deposition, the electrode was thoroughly rinsed with MilliQ water (18.2 Mohmcm) and left to dry in open air.

sections.heading: Anode Preparation
sections.text:
The anodes were synthesized by depositing a mixture of 9.5 mg of anhydrous IrO2 (43396, 99.99% metals basis, Alfa Aesar), 31 μL of Nafion solution, 400 μL of isopropyl alcohol and 400 μL of MilliQ water onto a gas diffusion layer (Sigracet 35 BC) using a paintbrush.
Prior to application the mixture was sonicated for 20 min. All the anodes had a final loading of 2.01 mgcm 2.[15]

sections.heading: Catalyst Characterization
sections.text: The electrodes prepared were examined with SEM to explore their surface morphology before and after the CO2 electroreduction process, using an acceleration voltage of 20 kV and an electron beam current of 126 μA. The diffraction patterns of the catalysts were collected in Bragg-Brentano reflection geometry with fixed irradiated area. Identification was performed by matching the measured diffraction pattern to the reference patterns contained in the Powder Diffraction File (PDF-4+ , edition 2018). All measurements were taken at room temperature. The method was issued to examine the crystalline structures of the catalysts. The ECSA was measured using the underpotential deposition method. A cyclic voltammogram was measured for each electrode in a solution of 0.1 M HClO4+0.0001 M Pb(ClO4)2 after reducing the surface to metallic copper. The potential range was set between 0.4 V and 0.1 V vs. Ag/AgCl to avoid the Pb bulk deposition peak that appears around 0.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl, at a 10 mVs 1 scan rate. The solution was purged with Ar for an hour prior to the experiment.

sections.heading: Electroreduction of CO2 in a Flow Electrolyzer
sections.text: The electrochemical reduction of the CO2 was conducted in a flow type electrolyzer, originally developed at the University of Illinois[16] (Figure S1), at room temperature and pressure. No membrane was used in any of the experiments. IrO2 on a GDL was used as anode and Ag/AgCl as reference electrode, connected externally to the cell. The electrolyte used was 1 M KOH (Merck). A CO2 (Air Gas) flow rate of 10 mLmin 1 was maintained over the cathode GDE using a flow controller (SLA5800 Series, Brooks Instrument). The electrolyte was set at a constant flow rate of 0.1 mLmin 1 and allowed to flow between the cathode and the anode using a pump (Stepdos 03RC, KNF Lab). The electrochemical experiments were performed at a constant cell voltage using a potentiostat (Autolab, Metrohm). After the operating cell voltage was turned on, the current was stabilized for at least 300 seconds before the GC analysis was performed. Since our electrochemical experiments were performed in a GDL based flow electrolyzer, we observed fluctuations in the current density over time due to bubble formation on the electrode surface. To accurately quantify the electrochemical results, the current was averaged over a 600 second time-period. The reference electrode was placed in the electrolyte stream near the electrolyzer inlet. All potentials reported in this work are the actual measured values without any iR correction unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: Product Analysis
sections.text:
The gaseous products were analysed using the thermal conductivity (TCD) and flame ionization detector (FID) mode channels of an on-line gas chromatograph (CGC4, Gas Analyser Solutions, Interscience) with a Molsieve 5 A, 60–80 column and an Al202/MAPD respectively. Hydrogen (H2) was analysed with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and N2 as the carrier gas. Other gas-phase products (CO, CH4, C2H6, C2H4, C3H8, C3H6) were analysed with a flame ionization detector (FID) and helium as the carrier gas. The retention time of the gas products was observed as following: H2 (0.726 min); CO (5.167 min); CH4 (0.612 min); C2H6 (0.677 min); C2H4 (0.777 min); C3H8 (0.969 min); C3H6 (1.55 min) and CO2 (1.757 min). Liquid phase products were analysed using an off-line HighPerformance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) and an off-line GC.
